qualificationsMath.analytic: An infinitary rule deriving q from all axioms p_n is closed in the least rule-closed set but has no finite derivation tree. Infinitely many disjoint height-two diamonds have infinitely many distinct local forks. These infinite conclusions follow from the explicit constructions, not a finite cutoff.

fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: An inference rule has premises (judgments) above a line and a conclusion below. A set of rules with finitely many premises per rule inductively defines a relation or predicate: the judgment JJJ holds exactly when it has a derivation, a finite tree whose root is JJJ, whose every node is the conclusion of a rule instance, and whose children are the premises of that instance (axioms have none). The set is the least one closed under the rules; the height of a derivation is a measure for induction on derivations.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: Reading rules top-down builds up the set (stage by stage: all conclusions whose premises were already derived); reading them bottom-up is proof search, as here: to derive JJJ, choose a rule whose conclusion has the right shape, and recursively derive its premises. A rule applied to a judgment of the wrong shape, or whose premises have no derivation, yields no tree at all.For the finitely premised rules used here, the stage construction makes this leastness precise. Put D0=∅D_0=\varnothingD0​=∅ and let Dn+1D_{n+1}Dn+1​ contain DnD_nDn​ and the conclusions of rules whose premises lie in DnD_nDn​. Mathematical induction (ALG 2.1) shows that every rule-closed set contains every DnD_nDn​. Conversely, finitely many premises in the union all occur by one common finite stage, so the union is rule closed. A second induction identifies stage membership with a finite derivation of bounded height. Thus the finite-tree and least-closed-set descriptions agree for these rules; an infinitary rule would require a different argument.

fields.text: Each rule strictly decreases the size of the term: the computation rules replace a term by one of its proper subterms (or by a constant), and a congruence rule shrinks the whole term because its premise shrinks a part (induction on the derivation of the step). A strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers is finite, and starting from size(t)\mathrm{size}(t)size(t) it cannot have more than size(t)−1\mathrm{size}(t)-1size(t)−1 steps. This is the first appearance of a termination measure; the argument collapses as soon as a rule can enlarge a term.The well-ordering principle (ALG 2.6) supplies the termination step, after the rules have been checked to decrease size. If an infinite run existed, the nonempty set of its positive integer sizes would have a least member; the next step would have an even smaller size, a contradiction. More quantitatively, after kkk steps the size is at most its starting size minus kkk, and the final term still has at least one node. This gives at most size(t)−1\mathrm{size}(t)-1size(t)−1 steps. Strict decrease among arbitrary positive real numbers would not suffice; the measure here is integer valued.

fields.label: statement-scope
fields.text: There are three classical ways to say what a program means. Operational semantics describes how it runs: a sequence of configurations produced by rules. Denotational semantics assigns it a mathematical object — for an imperative command, a partial function from initial stores to final stores, built by recursion on the syntax, with loops given by limits of approximations. Axiomatic semantics states what is true of it: a Hoare triple {P} c {Q}\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}{P}c{Q} says that if PPP holds before ccc and ccc terminates, then QQQ holds afterwards. The three are different questions about one program, and for the languages studied here they agree: the final state of a run is the denotation, and it satisfies every triple that is provable.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: Operational semantics is the specification an implementer follows; denotational semantics compares programs and gives compositional reasoning (the meaning of c1;c2c_1;c_2c1​;c2​ is the composite of the meanings); axiomatic semantics is tuned for proofs, replacing the infinite set of stores by assertions and a loop by an invariant. The links between them — the denotation of a loop is the least fixed point of its unrolling, a triple is valid if it holds on every run — are the subjects of chapter 10. Strachey and Scott's mathematical semantics, Floyd's and Hoare's program logics and Plotkin's rules all date from the 1960s–80s.Sequencing uses the associativity argument for composition (ALG 1.15), with partiality made explicit. Adjoin an undefined element ⊥\bot⊥ to the set of stores and extend each command denotation strictly by sending ⊥\bot⊥ to ⊥\bot⊥. These are total maps on the enlarged set. Both bracketings of three sequential commands follow the same three maps and are undefined in exactly the same cases, so their denotations agree. This supplies compositional sequencing, not the existence or adequacy of a loop's least fixed point. For first-order integer assertions, satisfaction (LOGIC 3.4) supplies the meaning of PPP and QQQ: use the fixed integer structure and the store as variable assignment. Partial correctness requires, for every initial store satisfying PPP, that every defined final store satisfy QQQ; it does not require termination. This is a statement about all stores, not just the finite test panel.

Identity renaming, reversing a safe renaming, and composing finite safe renamings give reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. If two such classes meet, the target's symmetry-and-transitivity argument makes them the same class, so every named term belongs to exactly one block. fields.text: Let →\to→ be a binary relation on a set (for us: →β\to_\beta→β​ on λ\lambdaλ-terms up to ≡α\equiv_\alpha≡α​) and →∗\to^{*}→∗ its reflexive–transitive closure. →\to→ has the diamond property if b←a→cb\leftarrow a\to cb←a→c implies there is ddd with b→d←cb\to d\leftarrow cb→d←c: one step on each side closes the fork. →\to→ is confluent if →∗\to^{*}→∗ has the diamond property, i.e. whenever a→∗ba\to^{*}ba→∗b and a→∗ca\to^{*}ca→∗c there is ddd with b→∗db\to^{*}db→∗d and c→∗dc\to^{*}dc→∗d. The diamond property implies confluence (tile a grid of diamonds), but not conversely. →β\to_\beta→β​ is confluent (3.4), yet it does not have the diamond property: contracting a redex can copy or erase another one, so the fork may need several steps to close on one side.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: Confluence is the statement that the choices made by a reduction strategy (2.5) never matter in the long run: whatever two partial computations have been done from the same term, both can still be completed to the same term. If the relation has the diamond property one proves confluence by induction on the lengths of the two paths, filling in a grid one diamond at a time. For β\betaβ the single diamond is false, as the duplicating redex (λx. x x) ((λy. y) z)(\lambda x.\,x\,x)\,((\lambda y.\,y)\,z)(λx.xx)((λy.y)z) shows: contracting the outer redex copies the inner one, which then needs two further steps, while the other side needs one. Closing that gap is the job of parallel reduction (3.3).The grid argument uses mathematical induction (ALG 2.1) on two finite path lengths. First induct on the length of one path to commute a single step past it, adjoining one diamond at a time. Then induct on the number of steps in the other path, applying that strip construction to each successive step. An empty path is the base case and needs only the other path as a joining sequence. This proves confluence from the stated one-step diamond property; it does not assume that ordinary beta reduction has that stronger property or replace its parallel-reduction argument.

fields.text: There are three classical ways to say what a program means. Operational semantics describes how it runs: a sequence of configurations produced by rules. Denotational semantics assigns it a mathematical object — for an imperative command, a partial function from initial stores to final stores, built by recursion on the syntax, with loops given by limits of approximations. Axiomatic semantics states what is true of it: a Hoare triple {P} c {Q}\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}{P}c{Q} says that if PPP holds before ccc and ccc terminates, then QQQ holds afterwards. The three are different questions about one program, and for the languages studied here they agree: the final state of a run is the denotation, and it satisfies every triple that is provable.

fields.text: There are three classical ways to say what a program means. Operational semantics describes how it runs: a sequence of configurations produced by rules. Axiomatic semantics states what is true of it: a Hoare triple {P} c {Q}\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}{P}c{Q} says that if PPP holds before ccc and ccc terminates, then QQQ holds afterwards. The three are different questions about one program, and for the languages studied here they agree: the final state of a run is the denotation, and it satisfies every triple that is provable.

fields.text: There are three classical ways to say what a program means. Operational semantics describes how it runs: a sequence of configurations produced by rules. Denotational semantics assigns it a mathematical object — for an imperative command, a partial function from initial stores to final stores, built by recursion on the syntax, with loops given by limits of approximations. Axiomatic semantics states what is true of it: a Hoare triple {P} c {Q}\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}{P}c{Q} says that if PPP holds before ccc and ccc terminates, then QQQ holds afterwards. The three are different questions about one program, and for the languages studied here they agree: the final state of a run is the denotation, and it satisfies every triple that is provable.

The links between them — the denotation of a loop is the least fixed point of its unrolling, a triple is valid if it holds on every run — are the subjects of chapter 10. fields.text: There are three classical ways to say what a program means. Operational semantics describes how it runs: a sequence of configurations produced by rules. Denotational semantics assigns it a mathematical object — for an imperative command, a partial function from initial stores to final stores, built by recursion on the syntax, with loops given by limits of approximations. Axiomatic semantics states what is true of it: a Hoare triple {P} c {Q}\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}{P}c{Q} says that if PPP holds before ccc and ccc terminates, then QQQ holds afterwards. The three are different questions about one program, and for the languages studied here they agree: the final state of a run is the denotation, and it satisfies every triple that is provable.

fields.label: proof
fields.text: Operational semantics is the specification an implementer follows; denotational semantics compares programs and gives compositional reasoning (the meaning of c1;c2c_1;c_2c1​;c2​ is the composite of the meanings); axiomatic semantics is tuned for proofs, replacing the infinite set of stores by assertions and a loop by an invariant. The links between them — the denotation of a loop is the least fixed point of its unrolling, a triple is valid if it holds on every run — are the subjects of chapter 10. Strachey and Scott's mathematical semantics, Floyd's and Hoare's program logics and Plotkin's rules all date from the 1960s–80s.Sequencing uses the associativity argument for composition (ALG 1.15), with partiality made explicit. Adjoin an undefined element ⊥\bot⊥ to the set of stores and extend each command denotation strictly by sending ⊥\bot⊥ to ⊥\bot⊥. These are total maps on the enlarged set. Both bracketings of three sequential commands follow the same three maps and are undefined in exactly the same cases, so their denotations agree. This supplies compositional sequencing, not the existence or adequacy of a loop's least fixed point. For first-order integer assertions, satisfaction (LOGIC 3.4) supplies the meaning of PPP and QQQ: use the fixed integer structure and the store as variable assignment. Partial correctness requires, for every initial store satisfying PPP, that every defined final store satisfy QQQ; it does not require termination. This is a statement about all stores, not just the finite test panel.

fields.text: Computation is nothing but the repeated contraction of redexes, each time substituting the argument for the parameter (2.3). Because redexes can be nested or disjoint, the order is a choice, and the graph of reachable terms records all choices.
